title: Hiccups Lasting Over Two Days Have a Medical Name, and One Smoker's Hidden Lung Abscess Shows Why
text:
Hiccups Lasting Over Two Days Have a Medical Name, and One Smoker's Hidden Lung Abscess Shows Why
Most hiccups disappear before anyone thinks twice about them. Once they last more than 48 hours, doctors stop calling them ordinary and classify them as persistent. That threshold mattered for a 65-year-old man in Lebanon whose four days of persistent hiccups turned out to be his body's only obvious signal of a pus-filled cavity in his lung.
Physicians affiliated with Lebanon's University of Balamand described the case in Clinical Medicine Insights: Case Reports, under the title "When Hiccups Speak Louder Than Cough." Their takeaway applies well beyond one patient: "Persistent hiccups may be the sole presenting symptom of serious thoracic pathology."
A Lung Infection Without the Usual Warning Signs
The man smoked a pack a day but had no other medical history. He came in with four days of hiccups and "reported no fever, chills, cough, chest pain, hemoptysis, or night sweats." His vital signs were stable.
There were quieter clues. On exam, doctors heard mildly decreased air entry over the right middle and lower lobes. His C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, was 297 mg/L, far above the normal level of under 10. His white blood cell count was mildly raised, with neutrophils, the infection-fighting cells that respond to bacteria, making up 81.3% of the total.
A CT scan showed consolidation in the back portion of the right lower lobe with a cavity about 2.8 centimeters wide containing an air-fluid level, the classic look of a lung abscess. The Cleveland Clinic describes a lung abscess as "a collection of pus in your lungs caused by a bacterial infection," with symptoms that can include fever, cough, and coughing up foul-smelling mucus or pus. This patient reported neither fever nor cough.
The scan also showed enlarged lymph nodes in the center of the chest, which in a long-time smoker raised the question of cancer. Bronchoscopy, a camera exam of the airways, found no tumor in the airway, and tests on the samples were negative for tuberculosis and cancer cells. A follow-up CT a week later found no infection or signs of cancer spread in the abdomen. A PCR test on fluid washed from his lungs identified Klebsiella pneumoniae. The CDC notes that these bacteria can cause pneumonia and bloodstream infections, and that "healthy people usually do not get Klebsiella infections." The agency also warns that resistance to carbapenems, a class of last-line antibiotics, is increasing among these bacteria. His strain was susceptible to fluoroquinolones in lab testing.
Six Weeks and Three Antibiotics
Treatment did not go smoothly, partly because he was already known to be allergic to penicillin. He started on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam, but it was stopped after one day because of an allergic reaction. He then received intravenous levofloxacin for 48 hours. When his inflammatory markers remained elevated, doctors switched him to tigecycline for two weeks.
He went home on oral levofloxacin to complete six weeks of antibiotics in total. His CRP fell from 297 to 26, and follow-up imaging showed the abscess had nearly resolved. By discharge, his hiccups were gone. The paper does not mention any hiccup-specific medication, which suggests treating the infection was what mattered. The Cleveland Clinic notes that lung abscesses often need antibiotics for "weeks or even months."
The authors explain the hiccups through anatomy. The hiccup reflex runs through the phrenic and vagus nerves, which carry signals between the diaphragm, chest, and brain. The right lower lobe sits "in close proximity to the diaphragm," and the authors propose the abscess irritated the diaphragm or the ends of the right phrenic nerve, setting off the reflex again and again.
That explanation is the authors' interpretation, supported by the hiccups ending as the infection cleared, but a single case cannot prove it.
Where Persistent Hiccups Come From
According to StatPearls, a clinical reference hosted by the National Library of Medicine, acute hiccups last under 48 hours, persistent hiccups last longer than two days, and intractable hiccups go on for more than a month.
The list of possible causes is long because so many structures touch the reflex pathway. StatPearls lists pneumonia, pleuritis, pulmonary embolism, empyema, and tumors among chest causes. Gastroesophageal reflux disease is associated with as many as 80% of persistent cases. Medications, nervous system disorders, and metabolic problems are also on the list.
MedicalDaily has reported other cases that fit this pattern, including a man whose five days of hiccups led doctors to a tumor on his phrenic nerve, and hiccups that began after a spinal steroid injection.
When Hiccups Are Worth a Doctor's Visit
Hiccups are extremely common, and the vast majority are harmless and brief. This case does not mean a hiccup fit signals lung disease.
The Lebanese team's point is narrower. Hiccups that last beyond two days are a medical symptom in their own right and deserve an explanation, especially in someone with risk factors like smoking or with subtle findings such as abnormal breath sounds or high inflammatory markers.
Anyone with hiccups lasting more than 48 hours, or with hiccups accompanied by trouble breathing, chest pain, fever, or difficulty eating, should contact a clinician.
Key Questions Answered
When do hiccups become a medical concern?
Hiccups lasting more than 48 hours are classified as persistent, and those lasting over a month are intractable. Both warrant medical evaluation.
What caused this man's hiccups?
His doctors linked them to a 2.8 cm abscess in the right lower lung, near the diaphragm, caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae.
Why didn't he have a cough or fever?
The authors note that older adults can have a blunted inflammatory response, so a serious infection may not cause fever. The case shows a lung abscess can appear without its typical symptoms.
How was he treated?
With a sequence of antibiotics over six weeks, after an allergic reaction forced an early switch. The abscess nearly resolved.
What are common causes of persistent hiccups?
Acid reflux is the most commonly cited, along with chest infections, nerve irritation, medications, and nervous system or metabolic disorders.
Should people worry about ordinary hiccups?
No. Most hiccups are brief and harmless. Persistent hiccups, or hiccups with other symptoms, should be checked by a clinician.
